notes.b: Gaelic football is an invasion game (a game where teams move into the opponents' territory to score). Its skills are handling, moving with the ball, kicking and tackling, and each has a few coaching points you should be able to name.
points: Catching: to catch a high ball, make a W shape with the hands and spread the fingers, which gives the widest possible surface to take the ball.
Hand pass: hold the ball in one hand and strike it with the fist or open palm. It is struck, not thrown, so the ball must leave the hand from a strike, such as with the fist.
Soloing (running with the ball while keeping it in your control): drop the ball onto the foot and kick it back to the hands while running.
Toe-to-hand pick-up: lift the ball off the ground with the toe and catch it in the hands. This is how the ball is lifted, because it may not be picked up with the hands.
Kicking from the hands: keep the eyes on the ball, place the non-kicking foot beside the ball's line, and follow through towards the target.
Tackling and blocking: the shoulder-to-shoulder tackle (making contact shoulder to shoulder with the player who has the ball), and blocking (getting a hand or body in the way of the ball).
notes.tip: Gaelic football is one of the games that appears repeatedly in exams, so be ready to name each skill and give its coaching points, such as the W-shaped catch or the foot beside the ball when kicking.

notes.b: The rules limit how long a player can carry the ball and how it can be moved, so a player who wants to keep the ball must keep moving it in a permitted way.
points: A player may hold the ball for a maximum of four steps before it must be soloed, bounced or released (passed or kicked away).
The ball may not be bounced twice in a row, but soloing may be repeated as often as the player likes.
The ball may not be picked directly off the ground with the hands, so a player must use the toe-lift (toe-to-hand pick-up) instead.

notes.b: Hurling and camogie are played with a hurley (a wooden stick with a curved, flat end called the bas). The skills are about controlling the ball with the stick and the hand, and tackling safely.
points: Ready position: hold the hurley with the dominant hand at the top of the hurley, so you are set to strike or lift.
Pick-up: the ball is lifted from the ground with a roll lift or a jab lift, because it may not be picked up directly by hand.
Catching: catch the ball with the hand protected, so that the hand is not hurt by the ball or the hurleys.
Soloing: run while the ball is balanced on the bas of the hurley.
Striking from the hand and off the ground: keep the hands together for power, or apart for control.
Tackling: the hook (using the hurley to pull or knock the opponent's stick off the ball) and the block (placing the hurley in the way of the strike).
Hand pass: the ball is struck with the palm, so it is hit, not thrown.
notes.tip: Hurling is one of the games that appears repeatedly in exams. When asked about striking, say hands together for power and hands apart for control.

notes.b: Handling in hurling and camogie is limited, so players must use the hurley to lift the ball and cannot run far with it in the hand.
points: The ball may be carried in the hand for a maximum of four steps.
The ball may not be picked directly off the ground with the hand; a lift (roll lift or jab lift, using the hurley) is used instead.

notes.b: Rugby union is an invasion game in which the ball is passed backwards while the team advances. The skills cover passing, tackling, keeping the ball in contact situations and evading defenders.
points: Rugby passes go backwards or level, never forwards. A pass that goes forward is a forward pass, which is an infringement (a breach of the rules).
Receiving: hold the hands up as a target for the passer, so they can see where to aim, with the fingers spread to catch the ball securely.
Spin pass: used to gain distance, because the spin helps the ball travel further.
Tackling: go cheek to cheek (head to the side of the ball carrier), put the shoulder into the thigh, and wrap the arms around the ball carrier.
Tackling finish: drive with the legs, which keeps the tackle moving forwards, then finish on top of the ball carrier.
Maul (a contest for the ball while it is held off the ground by the ball carrier): the ball carrier stays on their feet, for example while team-mates bind on to them.
Ruck (a contest for the ball after a tackle): the ball is on the ground, and players bind (grip each other) and stay on their feet.
Evasion (getting past a defender while carrying the ball): use the side-step and the swerve, which change your direction so the defender misses you.
notes.tip: Remember that rugby passes go backwards or level, never forwards. If a question asks about a pass, do not describe it going forward.

notes.b: Two infringements and two tackle rules decide whether play is legal.
points: Infringements: a forward pass (the ball thrown forward) and a knock-on (the ball knocked or dropped forward from the hands) are both rule breaches.
Tackles must be below the shoulders, and the tackler must release the ball carrier after the tackle.

notes.b: Basketball is an invasion game in which players move the ball by passing and dribbling (bouncing the ball while moving) and score by shooting into the basket. Each skill has set coaching points.
points: Chest pass: release with the thumbs down and step into the pass, which adds power.
Bounce pass: bounce the ball two-thirds of the way to the receiver.
Overhead pass: pass the ball from above the head, so it travels over a defender's reach.
Dribbling: use the fingertips, keep the ball below the waist so it is hard to steal, keep the eyes up to see the court, and protect the ball with the body.
Lay-up (a shot taken close to the basket while moving): a right-hand lay-up is taken off the left foot, after two steps.
Set and jump shot: use the BEEF cue, which stands for balance, eyes on the target, elbow under the ball and follow-through.
Rebounding (winning the ball after a missed shot): box out the opponent to win position under the basket.
Defensive stance: stay low with the feet shoulder-width apart, sliding without crossing the feet, because crossing the feet makes you unbalanced.
notes.tip: Basketball is one of the games that appears repeatedly in exams. If a question asks for a shooting cue, give BEEF and say what each letter stands for.

notes.b: A player with the ball who is not dribbling must follow footwork and time rules. Breaking them gives possession to the other team.
points: Pivot footwork: keep one foot planted while turning on the other, so you can turn without travelling.
Travelling: moving the pivot foot, or taking too many steps while holding the ball without dribbling. This is why a player must dribble or pass to move.
Double dribble: dribbling with both hands at once, or starting a new dribble after stopping one.
Three seconds: an attacking player may not stay in the key (the restricted area near the basket) for more than three seconds.
Personal fouls: illegal contact, such as pushing, holding or charging, gives the opponent possession or free throws (unopposed shots at the basket).

notes.b: Outfield players are all players except the goalkeeper. Their skills are passing, controlling, dribbling, shooting, heading and defending.
points: Inside-of-the-foot pass: lock the ankle, place the standing foot beside the ball, and follow through to the target.
Lofted pass and chip: the ball is lifted into the air to pass over the defence.
Cushioning control: the foot gives on contact to absorb the ball's pace, so the ball stays under control.
Dribbling: use both feet, with changes of pace, so a defender cannot predict your next touch.
Shooting with the laces: head over the ball and the non-kicking foot beside it.
Heading: use the forehead, with the eyes open, so you can see the ball and meet it cleanly.
Defending: jockeying (stay goal-side, between the attacker and your goal, stay side-on, and delay the attacker) and the block tackle.
notes.tip: Soccer is one of the games that appears repeatedly in exams. For defending, give all three parts of jockeying: goal-side, side-on and delay.

notes.b: The goalkeeper is the only player allowed to use the hands, so the skills are different from the rest of the team.
points: Set position: the goalkeeper is balanced and ready before the shot.
Catching: use a W-shaped catch for high balls and a scoop for low balls.
Diving: dive with the body behind the ball, so the body is a second barrier if the hands miss.
Narrowing the angle: move out towards the shooter, which leaves less of the goal to aim at.
Punching crosses (balls played in from the side): punch the ball away.
Distribution (getting the ball to a team-mate): by throw, roll and kick.

notes.b: Three rules shape how soccer is played: who may handle the ball, the offside rule and fouls.
points: Only the goalkeeper may handle the ball, and only inside their own penalty area.
Offside: a player is offside if, when the ball is played to them, they are in the opponents' half and nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last defender.
Fouls such as tripping, pushing or a careless tackle give a free kick, or a penalty if committed by a defender in their own penalty area.

notes.b: Netball is an invasion game with strict rules about contact and movement. Players hold the ball only briefly, so they must pass it on.
points: Passing: chest, shoulder, bounce and lob passes.
Footwork: land on one foot and pivot (turn on the spot); do not step with the landing foot.
Shooting: hold the ball on the fingertips above the head, with the knees bent for power, and use a flick of the wrist.
Dodging: a quick move to get free of the marker (the defender guarding you), so you can receive a pass.
Marking: arms out, 0.9 m (3 feet) from the player being marked.
Key rules: a player may hold the ball for no more than three seconds.
Key rules: no contact, and playing areas by position, which means each position is limited to certain areas of the court.

notes.b: Hockey is played with a stick that has a flat side and a rounded side, and only the flat side may be used. Skills cover grip, passing, dribbling, flicking, shooting and defending.
points: Grip: left hand at the top of the stick, right hand lower down.
Passing and stopping: the push pass, slap and hit; stop the ball on the open stick.
Dribbling: with the open stick and with the reverse stick.
Flicks: a lifting stroke used to move the ball off the ground, for example over a defender's stick.
Shooting: hit the ball towards goal from inside the shooting circle (the D-shaped area in front of the goal).
Defending: jockeying and channelling, which means forcing the attacker away from goal.
notes.tip: In hockey only the flat (face) side of the stick is used. Say this when asked about a rule or about technique.

notes.b: Hockey has three rules about how the stick is used and where goals can be scored.
points: In hockey only the flat (face) side of the stick is used.
Goals may only be scored from inside the shooting circle.
No dangerous play with the ball or stick.
notes.tip: In hockey only the flat (face) side of the stick is used. Do not say that either side can be used.

notes.b: The hockey goalkeeper wears protective kit and uses the pads and feet to stop shots.
points: Protective kit is worn by the goalkeeper, so shots can be stopped with the body.
Kicking clearances: the goalkeeper kicks the ball away from goal.
Saves are made with the pads and kickers (the protective boots worn over the feet).
Defending short corners (a set play awarded to the attackers near the goal).
Facing penalty flicks (a flick taken at the goal as a penalty).
Diving and sliding saves.

notes.b: Olympic handball is an invasion game played with the hands, where players pass and shoot at a goal. Players must keep moving the ball because they may hold it only briefly.
points: Catching: the hands form a W.
Passing: one-handed passes.
Shooting: a jump shot from outside the goal area, and the penalty throw.
Moving free: getting clear of a marker so that a team-mate can pass to you.
Defending: marking in a zone (each defender guards an area).
Key rules: a maximum of three steps and three seconds holding the ball.
Key rules: only the goalkeeper may stand in the goal area.

keyTerms.definition: Dropping the ball onto the foot and kicking it back up to the hands while running.
Lifting the ball off the ground with the toe and catching it in the hands.
Striking a ball held in one hand with the fist or open palm, rather than throwing it.
Positioning the body between an opponent and the basket to win a rebound.
A close-range basketball shot taken off the foot opposite the shooting hand after two steps.
A basketball shooting cue for balance, eyes on the target, elbow under the ball and follow-through.
Keeping one foot planted while turning on the other.
A rugby union contest in which the ball carrier stays on their feet while players bind around them.
A rugby union contest for the ball on the ground, in which players bind and stay on their feet.
A rugby union infringement in which the ball is knocked forward with the hand or arm.
Keeping an attacker goal-side and side-on, delaying them until help arrives.
Directing an attacker away from goal, towards an area where they can be dispossessed.

factCards.definition: A maximum of four steps holding the ball before it must be soloed, bounced or released.
A maximum of four steps with the ball carried in the hand; the ball may not be picked directly off the ground with the hand.
No more than three seconds holding the ball.
A maximum of three steps and three seconds holding the ball.

factCards.term: Hockey: which side of the stick
factCards.definition: Only the flat (face) side of the stick may be used.
Passes go backwards or level only; a forward pass is an infringement.

questions.prompt: Describe two skills from an invasion game of your choice, giving key technique points for each.
questions.model: Activity: Gaelic football. Skill one, kicking from the hands: the player keeps their eyes on the ball, places the non-kicking foot beside the line of the ball, and strikes through it, following through towards the target, so the kick has accuracy and direction. Skill two, the hand pass: the ball is held in one hand and struck with the fist or open palm rather than thrown, so the pass can be delivered quickly to a team-mate in a tight space, without losing control of the ball.

questions.prompt: Describe the lay-up in basketball and explain how a coach could use part practice to teach it.
questions.model: Lay-up: a right-hand lay-up is taken off the left foot after two steps. The player gathers the ball, takes two steps towards the basket, jumps off the left foot and places the ball up towards the basket with the right hand. Part practice: the coach isolates one sub-routine of the lay-up and practises it alone before the whole skill. First the footwork, two steps and a jump off the left foot, is practised without the ball. Next the ball handling is added, with a gather and a catch while stepping. Then the release is practised on its own, placing the ball up with the right hand. When each part is secure, the coach puts them back together and the player performs the whole lay-up.

questions.prompt: Outline three rules of a named invasion game that affect how players move with the ball.
questions.model: Gaelic football. First, a player may hold the ball for a maximum of four steps before it must be soloed, bounced or released. Second, the ball may not be bounced twice in a row, although soloing may be repeated. Third, the ball may not be picked directly off the ground with the hands; the toe-lift is used instead.
